nameStory: The name 'pot marigold' comes from its historical use in cooking pots - the edible petals were added to soups and stews as both flavoring and golden coloring. 'Mary's gold' refers to the golden crown of the Virgin Mary, as English people named this sunny flower to honor her. The 'pot' also distinguishes it from other marigolds that aren't typically used in cooking.
description: Pot marigold is a cheerful annual flower with bright orange or yellow daisy-like blooms that seem to glow in the garden. The plants grow in low, bushy mounds about 12-18 inches tall and wide, with soft, light green leaves. Originally from southern Europe, this old-fashioned garden flower has been cultivated for so long that it sometimes escapes cultivation and pops up in wild spaces. The flowers have a distinctive, slightly spicy scent that's quite pleasant when you brush against them.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright orange or yellow daisy-like flowers, 2-3 inches across, with numerous narrow petals radiating from a darker center. The petals feel slightly waxy and have a mild, pleasant spicy scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, light green leaves that are lance-shaped with smooth or slightly toothed edges. They alternate up the stem and feel somewhat fuzzy or downy to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, bushy plants that spread in mounded clumps, rarely getting taller than 18 inches. Stems are somewhat succulent and break easily when bent.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Curved, hook-shaped seeds that look almost like tiny crescents or question marks. They're light brown and have a distinctive sculptural appearance unlike typical daisy family seeds.

habitat: In New England, pot marigold is most commonly found in home gardens, herb gardens, and around old farmsteads where it has escaped cultivation. It occasionally appears in disturbed soils along roadsides, in vacant lots, or near compost piles. It prefers well-drained, moderately fertile soil and full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Seeds can be planted in early spring, and young plants emerge with their characteristic soft, light green leaves in a rosette pattern.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with bright orange and yellow flowers opening continuously from early summer through fall. Flowers open in the morning and may close during very hot afternoons.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until hard frost, often looking its best in the cooler temperatures of early fall. Seeds mature and drop, potentially creating new plants next year.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die with frost, leaving behind curved seeds that may overwinter in the soil to germinate next spring.

funFact: The petals of pot marigold are completely edible and were once used as a cheaper substitute for expensive saffron, earning it the nickname 'poor man's saffron' - the petals give rice and soups a beautiful golden color and a slightly peppery flavor!
confusionNotes: Often confused with common garden marigolds (Tagetes), but pot marigolds have softer, more daisy-like flowers and light green foliage, while Tagetes marigolds have more ruffled, dense flower heads and darker, more pungent-smelling leaves. Remember: pot marigolds smell pleasant and spicy, Tagetes marigolds smell sharp and skunky.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the common garden marigolds (Tagetes) sold at garden centers - they're completely different plants from different parts of the world. True pot marigolds belong to the daisy family and have been grown in European herb gardens for over 1,000 years, while Tagetes marigolds are from Mexico and Central America.
compareHints: Field marigold (Calendula arvensis), the only other Calendula species you might encounter, has much smaller, paler yellow flowers and grows as a weedy annual in agricultural areas. Pot marigold's flowers are notably larger, more vibrant in color, and the plant has a much more robust, garden-worthy appearance. Field marigold also has a more sprawling, less tidy growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field marigold differs from its more common relative, pot marigold (Calendula officinalis), by being smaller overall with more delicate stems and smaller flower heads.
